The correct limit is 1/10, so none of the three solutions is right.

**The graph.** Write each vertex as a pair (i, j) with i < j. Its neighbours are (i±1, j) and (i, j±1), whenever the result is still a valid pair. So T₂(Pₙ) is the induced subgraph of the square grid on the staircase region i < j. It has about n²/2 vertices, and the boundary of the region has only O(n) vertices.

**The limit.** The infinite square grid has domination density 1/5. Boundary effects contribute only O(n), so γ(T₂(Pₙ)) ≈ (1/5)(n²/2) = n²/10. The limit is therefore 1/10. This is an estimate from the grid density, not a full proof.

**Solution 1 (1/4).** Taking one colour class of the bipartition by parity of i + j gives a dominating set, but not a minimum one. The lower-bound argument fails. From |A| − x ≤ 4y and x + y < |A| it only follows that x ≥ |A| − 4/3 (for |A| ≥ 2), which does not lead to a contradiction. A degree-4 vertex dominates 5 vertices, not just the 4 neighbours it was credited with, so the bound is far from tight. The answer 1/4 is wrong.

**Solution 2 (1/6).** The set D₀ (pairs with j − i ≡ 0 mod 3) is dominating, but it is not minimal. The "lower bound" is only an appeal to cycle domination and is not a proof. The answer 1/6 is wrong.

**Solution 3 (1/8).** The solution itself expects about n²/10 from the grid density, then switches to an unsupported "observed" n²/8 with made-up small values. The answer 1/8 is wrong.

VERDICT 1: REJECT
VERDICT 2: REJECT
VERDICT 3: REJECT
